title: Validating XML with DTD

content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore validating xml with dtd within DTD and XML Document Validation. You will connect its syllabus topics to an inspectable example, check the expected result, and note tool/version limits.
content.why_it_matters: Validating XML with DTD matters because XML workflows rely on explicit structure and predictable processing. The lesson helps you reason about well-formedness versus dtd validity, avoid a common misunderstanding, and make a result reproducible for another developer.

content_blocks.title: Validating XML with DTD: concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Concept flow covering Well-formedness versus DTD validity, Parser-based validation, Reading validation errors, Maintaining DTD definitions.
content_blocks.caption: The visual introduces validating xml with dtd; inspect the worked example and then verify it.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A DTD describes permitted element content, attributes, and entity declarations. Validation checks that a well-formed XML document follows those declarations; DTDs have limited data typing and namespace modeling compared with XSD.

content_blocks.title: Connect the subtopics
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly covers: Well-formedness versus DTD validity; Parser-based validation; Reading validation errors; Maintaining DTD definitions. Treat these as connected parts of one workflow: define the structure, make the relevant assumptions explicit, and verify a result with a small known input.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Validating XML with DTD
content_blocks.code:
<!DOCTYPE catalog [
  <!ELEMENT catalog (product*)>
  <!ELEMENT product (name, price)>
  <!ELEMENT name (#PCDATA)>
  <!ELEMENT price (#PCDATA)>
]>
<catalog><product><name>Notebook</name><price>4.50</price></product></catalog>
content_blocks.expected_output: The document is well-formed and can be checked against the local DTD content model. Do not enable external DTD resolution for untrusted input.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this example as text. Run it only in a processor that supports the shown language/version; the standard CodeLeaf playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only and does not execute XML, XSD, XPath, XSLT, XQuery, Python, or SQL. Use small local DTDs to understand content models. External resource loading and entity expansion can create security and reliability risks, so avoid enabling them for untrusted XML by default.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the sample to its exact starting state before each experiment. Change one element, attribute, expression, or constraint at a time, then compare the result with the expected behavior.
content_blocks.limitations: This snippet is an inspectable example, not an XML execution service. Validate it with a standards-compatible XML processor; feature support depends on the processor/version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Distinguish well-formedness, schema validity, and application-level correctness; they are different checks.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small synthetic example that demonstrates “Well-formedness versus DTD validity”. Then add one boundary case involving “Parser-based validation”. Write down what should happen before testing, and record the exact output or processor message afterward.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a document is correct because it looks readable.
common_mistakes.why: Visual appearance does not prove well-formedness, schema validity, correct namespace handling, or application-level meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse and validate the document with the intended processor, then assert its meaning using a focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing specification features with processor support.
common_mistakes.why: A standard may define features that a specific runtime does not implement.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the version and feature support; test with the actual target processor.

common_mistakes.why: Missing values, wrong types, namespace differences, or boundary inputs can expose failures.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a valid case, an invalid case, and an edge case to the verification notes.
